name: Ahitub
title: Priest in Eli's lineage
summary: Ahitub belonged to the priestly lineage from Eli and was the son of Phinehas, who fell in battle against the Philistines when the ark of the covenant was captured. He was the brother of Ichabod, whose name testifies to the national crisis that struck Israel when God's glory departed from the sanctuary at Shiloh. Despite the catastrophe that befell his family – the loss of his father, grandfather, and the ark of the covenant – Ahitub continued the priestly tradition. He is regarded as the father of Abiathar, who wore the ephod in King Saul's service, and is also linked to Ahimelech, the priest at Nob, although it is debated whether Abiathar and Ahimelech were the same person or father and son. Ahitub thus appears as an important link in the priestly lineage that was eventually removed under Solomon in favor of Zadok, fulfilling the prophecy against the house of Eli. His name also appears in the priestly genealogies in Chronicles and in Ezra's genealogy, but there are several biblical figures with this name, making it challenging to distinguish them from one another.

keyEvents.title: Ahitub's lineage
keyEvents.description: Ahitub was the son of Phinehas and the grandson of Eli, the high priest who served at the tabernacle in Shiloh. He belonged to a priestly family that had responsibility for God's sanctuary.

keyEvents.title: Phinehas' Death and the Birth of Ichabod
keyEvents.description: Ahitub's father Phinehas died in the battle where the ark of the covenant was captured by the Philistines. Upon hearing this news, Phinehas' wife gave birth to a son named Ichabod, Ahitub's brother, and she named him because 'the glory has departed from Israel.' This crisis marked a turning point for the priestly lineage.

keyEvents.title: Ahitub as Father of Ahijah
keyEvents.description: Ahitub's son Ahijah served as a priest and carried the ephod during King Saul's reign, showing that the priestly line continued through Ahitub despite the crisis at Shiloh.

keyEvents.title: Ahimelech in Nob, Linked to Ahitub's Lineage
keyEvents.description: Ahimelech, described as the son of Ahitub, was the priest in Nob who gave David the showbread and Goliath's sword. Whether Ahimelech was identical to Ahijah or his son is debated. The event led Saul to kill the priests in Nob, a tragedy that severely impacted Eli's lineage.

keyEvents.title: Ahitub in the Priestly Genealogy of Chronicles
keyEvents.description: Ahitub is mentioned in the priestly genealogies in 1 Chronicles. There are several individuals named Ahitub in these lists, and scholars debate whether all references refer to the same person.

keyEvents.title: Ahitub in Ezra's Genealogy
keyEvents.description: Ahitub is mentioned in Ezra's genealogy, which traces the priestly succession through generations up to the return from the Babylonian exile.

versions.summary: Ahitub was an Israelite priest and son of Phinehas, grandson of Eli, the high priest at Shiloh. He is a key figure in the priestly lineage and father of Ahijah and Ahimelech, who served as priests during King Saul's time. Ahitub is also mentioned in later genealogies as part of the priestly succession leading up to temple service.
versions.title: Priestly Ancestor
versions.reason: [minor] The title 'Priestly Ancestor' is appropriate but could be made more precise by noting that he belonged to Eli's priestly lineage.; [major] The relationship between Ahijah and Ahimelech is debated. Many scholars believe Ahijah and Ahimelech may be the same person, or that Ahimelech was the son of Ahijah (not his brother). In 1 Sam 22:20, Abiathar is mentioned as the son of Ahimelech, son of Ahitub. In 1 Sam 14:3, Ahijah is mentioned as the son of Ahitub. It is possible that Ahijah and Ahimelech are the same person with two names, or that Ahimelech was the son of Ahijah. Both can still be retained as children of Ahitub based on a reading of the texts, but this should be noted in a footnote.; [major] 1 Sam 4:19-21 describes that it was Phinehas' wife (Ahitub's mother) who gave birth to a child named Ichabod, not Ahitub. Ahitub is Ichabod's brother (cf. 1 Sam 14:3 which gives the lineage Eli > Phinehas > Ahitub > Ahijah). The event concerning Phinehas' death is relevant, but the description should clarify that the child born at Phinehas' death was Ichabod, Ahitub's brother, not necessarily Ahitub himself.; [major] Ichabod was the brother of Ahitub (both sons of Phinehas). According to 1 Sam 4:19-21 and 14:3, Ichabod was a son of Phinehas, and Ahitub was also a son of Phinehas. Ichabod should be added as a sibling.; [minor] 1 Chr 6:7-8 and 6:11-12 refer to different Ahitubs in the genealogy. One is Ahitub the father of Zadok (in the Zadokite line), and the other is an Ahitub from a later generation. It should be clarified that there are multiple individuals named Ahitub in the genealogies, and there is debate over whether these refer to the same person.; [minor] Ezra 7:2 and 7:5 mention two different Ahitubs in the lineage. This should be commented on to avoid confusion.; [minor] The summary is good but should mention Ichabod as a brother and provide more nuance regarding the relationship between Ahijah and Ahimelech. It should also note that there are multiple individuals named Ahitub in the biblical genealogies.; [minor] 'judges' is reasonable for Ahitub himself, since he lived during the transition from the period of the judges to the monarchy. It could also be 'united-kingdom' given that his sons served under Saul, but 'judges' is acceptable for Ahitub himself.

versions.summary: Ahitub was an Israelite priest and son of Phinehas, grandson of Eli, the high priest in Shiloh. He was the brother of Ichabod, who was born when news of Phinehas' death and the capture of the ark reached their mother. Ahitub is a significant figure in the priestly lineage and is mentioned as the father of Ahijah, who wore the ephod during King Saul's time. He is also linked to Ahimelech, the priest at Nob, although it is debated whether Ahijah and Ahimelech were the same person or father and son. Ahitub is mentioned in the priestly genealogies in Chronicles and in Ezra's genealogy, but it is worth noting that there are several individuals named Ahitub in the biblical genealogies.
versions.title: Priest in Eli's lineage
versions.reason: [major] It is debated whether Ahimelek was the direct son of Akitub, or if he was the son of Ahia (and thus the grandson of Akitub). In 1 Sam 22:9, Ahimelek is referred to as 'son of Akitub', but in light of the discussion that Ahia and Ahimelek may be the same person (already mentioned in the summary), it is problematic to list both as children. If they are the same person, only one should be listed. If Ahimelek is the son of Ahia, he should not be listed as a child of Akitub. Since the biblical text in 1 Sam 22:9 actually calls Ahimelek 'son of Akitub', we should keep him but clarify the uncertainty. The safest approach is to list only Ahia as the direct child based on 1 Sam 14:3, and let the summary cover the relationship with Ahimelek.; [minor] Since this is version 2 and the previous version scored 5, the summary should be further improved. The text is good but can be strengthened with a bit more theological depth regarding Akitub's place in the broader narrative of Eli's lineage and its downfall.; [minor] 1 Chr 6:52 refers to the verse numbering in the Hebrew text. In many translations, this corresponds to a different verse (e.g., 6:37 in some numbering systems). The verse numbering in 1 Chr 6 varies between different traditions. Verses 7-8 and 11-12 are relevant, but verse 52 should be verified.; [minor] The footnotes are very good and comprehensive. The archaeological footnote about Shiloh is a great addition. A rabbinic footnote could further strengthen the profile.

footnotes.text: The name Ahitub (Hebrew: אֲחִיטוּב, Ahituv) means 'my brother is good' or 'brother of goodness.' This is a typical theophoric name from ancient Israel, where 'brother' can refer to a divine relative or protector.

There are at least two, possibly three, individuals named Ahitub in the biblical genealogies. One is the son of Phinehas and grandson of Eli (1 Sam 14:3), another is the father of Zadok who served under David (2 Sam 8:17; 1 Chr 6:7-8), and a third is mentioned in a later generation (1 Chr 6:11-12). Scholars debate whether any of these could be the same person.

The relationship between Ahijah and Ahimelech is debated among biblical scholars. Some believe they are the same person with two names (Ahijah = 'my brother is Yahweh', Ahimelech = 'my brother is king'). Others hold that Ahimelech was the son of Ahijah. The textual basis in 1 Samuel does not provide a completely clear solution.

Ichabod, Ahitub's brother, was born when news of the loss of the ark and Phinehas' death reached their mother. The name Ichabod (אִי־כָבוֹד) means 'no glory' or 'where is the glory?', and was given as an expression that God's glory had departed from Israel (1 Sam 4:19-22).

The priestly line of Eli served at the sanctuary in Shiloh, which archaeological excavations (Tell Seilun) have confirmed was destroyed around 1050 BC, likely by the Philistines. This aligns with the biblical account of the Philistine victory and the taking of the ark.

The priestly lineage from Eli through Ahitub was eventually removed when Solomon deposed Abiathar (Ahitub's grandson/great-grandson) from the priesthood (1 Kgs 2:26-27), replacing him with Zadok. This fulfilled the prophecy against the house of Eli in 1 Sam 2:27-36.

According to rabbinic tradition (Talmud, Zevachim 118b), the sanctuary at Shiloh was destroyed as punishment for Israel's sins, and this destruction marked the transition from a semi-permanent sanctuary to a more wandering existence for the ark of the covenant. For Ahitub's family, this meant a dramatic shift in their priestly service.
